blocks.body: Imagine searching through an unsorted database of N items for a specific target. Classically, you need to check items one by one — **O(N) queries** on average. Grover's algorithm (1996) finds the target in only **O(√N) queries**, a quadratic speedup.
Grover's speedup is provably optimal — no quantum algorithm can do better than O(√N) for unstructured search. This is one of the few known quantum lower bounds.
**1. Oracle (Oₓ):** Marks the target state |w⟩ by flipping its phase: |w⟩ → -|w⟩. All other states are unchanged.
**2. Diffusion (D):** Reflects all amplitudes about their mean. This *amplifies* the amplitude of the marked state.

blocks.latex: D = 2|s\rangle\langle s| - I \text{ where } |s\rangle = H^{\otimes n}|0\rangle^{\otimes n}

blocks.body: Think of the state vector in a 2D plane spanned by |w⟩ (target) and |s'⟩ (superposition of non-targets). Each Grover iteration rotates the state vector by angle 2θ toward |w⟩, where sin(θ) = 1/√N.
After π/(4θ) ≈ (π/4)√N iterations, the state is almost exactly |w⟩.
Searching for |11⟩ among 4 items (N=4). One Grover iteration suffices (π/4 · √4 ≈ 1.57 → 1 iteration):

blocks.caption: Grover's search for |11⟩ in a 2-qubit space — one iteration gives 100% success
stepDescriptions: H on q0: uniform superposition begins
Oracle CZ: marks |11⟩ with phase flip → amplitude of |11⟩ becomes negative
H on q0: begin diffusion operator
H on q1: diffusion — mapped to computational basis
Z on q0: conditional phase flip (part of reflection about |0⟩)
Z on q1: conditional phase flip
H on q0: map back from computational basis
H on q1: diffusion complete — |11⟩ now has probability 100%!

blocks.body: For the 2-qubit case (N=4), a single Grover iteration gives *perfect* amplification — the target state has 100% probability. For larger N, you need approximately (π/4)√N iterations.

Grover's algorithm is far more general than database search. It can speed up *any* problem where you can verify a solution efficiently. This includes satisfiability (SAT), constraint satisfaction, and even speeding up other algorithms as a subroutine (amplitude amplification). It also has implications for cryptography — it halves the effective key length of symmetric ciphers, which is why post-quantum security recommendations double key sizes.
